title: Git & GitHub Tutorial
body:
Git & GitHub Tutorial

Practical reference covering setup, cloning, committing, branching, restoring files, and CI/CD with GitHub Actions.

1. Connecting a New Project via HTTPS

Create an empty repo on GitHub (skip README/gitignore if your local folder already has files, to avoid a conflict on first push). Then inside your project folder:

  • git init
  • git add .
  • git commit -m "Initial commit"
  • git branch -M main
  • git remote add origin https://github.com/username/repo-name.git
  • git push -u origin main

Authentication note: GitHub no longer accepts your account password for HTTPS git operations. Git Credential Manager (bundled with Git for Windows) opens a browser login popup on first push and remembers you. Alternatively, generate a Personal Access Token under GitHub Settings, Developer settings, Personal access tokens, and paste it in place of your password when prompted.

2. Connecting to an Existing Project (Clone & Pull)

To clone a repo you don't have locally yet:

  • git clone https://github.com/username/repo-name.git
  • cd repo-name

To pull the latest changes into a repo you already have:

  • git pull origin main

If you already have a local folder not yet linked to the GitHub repo:

  • git remote add origin https://github.com/username/repo-name.git
  • git fetch origin
  • git checkout main

If your local folder has commits with no shared history, add --allow-unrelated-histories to the pull command.

3. Committing to GitHub

  • git status — see what's changed
  • git add <file> — stage a specific file
  • git add . — stage everything in the current directory
  • git commit -m "message" — commit staged changes
  • git push origin <branch> — push to GitHub

Commit message convention: feat: new feature, fix: bug fix, chore: maintenance/cleanup, docs: documentation only, refactor: code change that isn't a fix or feature, style: formatting only, test: adding or updating tests.

4. Branching

  • git checkout -b branch-name — create and switch in one step
  • git branch — list local branches
  • git checkout branch-name — switch to an existing branch
  • git push -u origin branch-name — push new branch, set upstream

Merge back via GitHub PR (recommended): push the branch, open a pull request into main, review the diff, then merge through the UI.

Or merge locally:

  • git checkout main
  • git pull origin main
  • git merge branch-name
  • git push origin main

Clean up after merge:

  • git branch -d branch-name
  • git push origin --delete branch-name

5. git restore

  • git restore <file> — discards uncommitted edits, reverts to last commit (also undoes an uncommitted deletion)
  • git restore --staged <file> — unstages a file, keeps the edits
  • git restore --source=<commit> <file> — restores a file's contents from a specific past commit

Only works on uncommitted changes. For already-committed/pushed changes, use git revert <commit> (safe for shared branches) or git reset (rewrites history, local-only commits).

Advanced: CI/CD with GitHub Actions

Workflows live in .github/workflows/*.yml. Basic example — lint and build on every push/PR to main:

  • on: push / pull_request, branches: [main]
  • jobs.build.runs-on: ubuntu-latest
  • steps: actions/checkout@v4
  • steps: actions/setup-node@v4 (node-version 20)
  • run: npm ci
  • run: npm run lint
  • run: npm run build

Secrets (API keys, DB URLs) go under repo Settings, Secrets and variables, Actions, referenced as ${{ secrets.YOUR_SECRET_NAME }} — never hardcoded in the YAML.

Branch protection (Settings, Branches) can require this workflow to pass before a PR merges into main, turning CI into an actual gate.

Deployment: on Vercel, connecting the GitHub repo auto-deploys every push and generates preview URLs per PR — no deploy step needed in Actions. For other hosts, add a final job gated to main using SSH/rsync/FTP actions, with needs: build so it waits for the build job to succeed first.

title: GitHub Tricks
body:
A quick reference for repository visualization, AI context, browser editors, GitHub URL patterns, and keyboard shortcuts. Replace user/repository, branch names, file paths, and pull request numbers with your own values.

Repository Tools & AI Context

1. GitDiagram — Visualize a repository

Replace github.com with gitdiagram.com to explore a repository as an interactive architecture diagram.

https://github.com/user/repository
https://gitdiagram.com/user/repository

Useful for understanding unfamiliar repositories, project structure, and relationships between modules before reading code.

2. GitIngest — Convert a repository into AI context

Replace github.com with gitingest.com to create a prompt-friendly text digest.

https://gitingest.com/user/repository

Output includes a directory tree, file contents, a summary, and copy/download options. Use file filters or target a folder when the repository is too large:

https://gitingest.com/user/repository/tree/main/src

CLI alternative:

pip install gitingest
gitingest https://github.com/user/repository

Example prompt to accompany the digest:

Audit this project's architecture.

Look for:
- unnecessary complexity
- duplicate code
- inconsistent naming
- security problems
- bad folder organization
- maintainability issues

3. DeepWiki — AI-generated repository documentation

https://deepwiki.com/user/repository

Useful for architecture explanations, learning unfamiliar codebases, and asking questions about a project. Documentation availability depends on repository indexing; verify generated explanations against the source.

4. GitHub.dev — Edit in browser-based VS Code

Replace github.com with github.dev, or press . while viewing a repository.

https://github.dev/user/repository

Useful for quick edits, code search, small commits, and reviews without cloning. This is a web editor, not a full compute environment for running builds or terminals.

5. GitHub1s — Browse with a VS Code-style interface

https://github1s.com/user/repository

Useful for reading code, exploring repositories, and navigating large folder structures.

6. GitMCP — Connect repository context to an AI assistant

https://gitmcp.io/user/repository

Configure this URL as a remote MCP server in a compatible assistant, such as Claude, Cursor, or Cline. GitMCP provides access to public repository documentation and code context without manually pasting everything.

Native GitHub URL Tricks

7. Get a raw file

Replace github.com with raw.githubusercontent.com and remove /blob/:

https://github.com/user/repository/blob/main/file.json
https://raw.githubusercontent.com/user/repository/main/file.json

Useful for downloading JSON, configuration files, scripts, and source files directly.

8. Compare branches or commits

https://github.com/user/repository/compare/main...dev
https://github.com/user/repository/compare/COMMIT1...COMMIT2

The three-dot comparison shows changes from the common ancestor to the second reference, rather than every difference between the two branch tips. Useful for reviewing proposed changes and investigating regressions.

9. Download a pull request as a diff

Append .diff to a pull request URL:

https://github.com/user/repository/pull/123.diff

Use the raw diff for focused code review. Example prompt:

Review this pull request.

Look for:
- bugs
- regressions
- security issues
- unnecessary complexity

10. Download a pull request as a patch

https://github.com/user/repository/pull/123.patch

A patch includes commit information alongside code changes. After downloading and reviewing it, check whether it applies cleanly:

git apply --check changes.patch

Use git apply changes.patch to apply changes without creating commits, or git am changes.patch to apply a mailbox-format patch as commits.

11. Link to specific code lines

Append a line anchor to a GitHub file URL:

  • file.ts#L20 — line 20.
  • file.ts#L20-L35 — lines 20 through 35.

Useful for reviews, documentation, bug reports, and sharing exact code.

12. Create a permanent code link

While viewing a file, press y. GitHub replaces the branch name in the URL with the exact commit SHA, pinning the link to that version instead of a moving branch.

/blob/main/src/file.ts
/blob/COMMIT_SHA/src/file.ts

Combine a commit-based URL with a line anchor for stable references in documentation, tutorials, and reviews.

13. View Markdown source

Append ?plain=1 to a Markdown file URL to inspect its source with line numbers. Add a line anchor when needed:

README.md?plain=1
README.md?plain=1#L20-L30

Folder Downloads

14. Download a single directory

Open the third-party tool https://download-directory.github.io/ and paste a GitHub folder URL:

https://github.com/user/repository/tree/main/assets

Useful when you only need /assets, /docs, /examples, or /templates instead of the full repository.

Browser Development Environments

15. StackBlitz

https://stackblitz.com/github/user/repository

Run compatible JavaScript, TypeScript, and Node-based web projects in a browser environment. Compatibility depends on the project's scripts, dependencies, and runtime requirements.

16. CodeSandbox

https://codesandbox.io/p/github/user/repository

Open GitHub projects for web development, demos, and reproducible environments. Sign-in, setup, or plan requirements may apply.

17. Gitpod

Historical repository-launch URL pattern:

https://gitpod.io/#https://github.com/user/repository

Used to launch cloud development environments without local setup. Check current Gitpod availability and launch instructions before relying on this legacy pattern.

File History

18. Git History — See how a file evolved

Replace github.com with github.githistory.xyz in a file URL:

https://github.com/user/repository/blob/main/file.js
https://github.githistory.xyz/user/repository/blob/main/file.js

Useful for examining when code was added, how implementations evolved, and how refactors changed a file.

GitHub Keyboard Shortcuts

  • . — open the repository in github.dev.
  • ? — show available keyboard shortcuts.
  • y — change the current file URL to a commit-based permalink.
  • t — open the repository file finder; type a filename such as package.json.
  • / — focus GitHub search.

Shortcuts depend on the current page and focus; use them outside text-entry fields.

Quick Tool Selection

  • See architecture: GitDiagram.
  • Read generated explanations: DeepWiki.
  • Prepare a code digest for AI: GitIngest.
  • Connect AI to repository context: GitMCP.
  • Browse source: GitHub1s.
  • Edit in the browser: github.dev.
  • Run a compatible web project: StackBlitz or CodeSandbox.
  • Inspect a file's evolution: Git History.

Suggested Workflow for an Unfamiliar Repository

  1. Use GitDiagram to get a visual overview.
  2. Read DeepWiki explanations and check them against the source.
  3. Use GitIngest to prepare only the code needed for your AI task.
  4. Inspect specific files with github.dev or GitHub1s.
  5. Configure GitMCP if your AI workflow needs ongoing repository context.

Privacy & Security

GitDiagram, GitIngest, DeepWiki, GitHub1s, GitMCP, Download Directory, StackBlitz, CodeSandbox, Gitpod, and Git History are third-party services. Availability, supported repositories, and access requirements can change.

  • Check requested GitHub permissions and avoid unnecessary organization-wide access.
  • For private repositories, confirm service support, authorization, retention policies, and whether sharing the code is permitted.
  • Exclude secrets before sending repository contents or diffs to external tools or AI services.
  • Never upload API keys, tokens, or secret-bearing .env files. Keep real secrets out of version control; use .env.example with placeholders.
  • Review unfamiliar code, patches, and setup scripts before applying or running them.
